title: Maximum Product of Three Numbers
description:
# Maximum Product of Three Numbers

Given an integer array `nums`, choose three numbers from the array so that their product is as large as possible. Return that maximum product.

Select three different indices; equal values are allowed when the input contains enough occurrences.

## Example 1:

**Input:** nums = [1,2,3]
**Output:** 6

## Example 2:

**Input:** nums = [1,2,3,4]
**Output:** 24

## Example 3:

**Input:** nums = [-1,-2,-3]
**Output:** -6

## Constraints:

* `3 <= nums.length <= 10^4`
* `-1000 <= nums[i] <= 1000`

solutions.name: One-Pass Five-Extrema Scan
solutions.description:
## Approach

Scan the array once while maintaining the three largest values and the two smallest values. At the end, compare `max1 * max2 * max3` with `min1 * min2 * max1`.

## Key Insight

Any maximum product of three numbers must use the largest positive factor available. The only way smaller numbers can help is when the two smallest values are both negative and become a large positive multiplier.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Sort and Compare End Candidates
solutions.description:
## Approach

Sort the array. Then the only two candidate products are the last three values, or the first two values with the last value.

## Key Insight

Sorting makes the extreme values visible. The maximum product either takes the largest three numbers directly, or uses the two most negative numbers to create a positive factor before multiplying by the largest number.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n log n)
- Space Complexity: O(1) extra space, ignoring the sorting implementation

solutions.name: Fixed-Size Heaps for Extremes
solutions.description:
## Approach

Keep a min-heap of the three largest values and a max-heap of the two smallest values. Each heap is capped at constant size while scanning the array.

## Key Insight

The problem only needs five extreme values, not a full sorted order. Small fixed-size heaps are a useful online pattern when a stream must retain a few largest and smallest elements.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n), because heap sizes are constant
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Bounded Value Counting Buckets
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use the constraint `-1000 <= nums[i] <= 1000` to count occurrences of each value. Sweep the bucket range from high to low to collect the three largest values, and from low to high to collect the two smallest values.

## Key Insight

When the value range is small and fixed, counting sort ideas can recover the needed extremes without comparison sorting. Here `V = 2001`, so the bucket cost is effectively constant for this problem's constraints.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n + V), where `V = 2001`
- Space Complexity: O(V)

solutions.name: Max-Min Product Dynamic Programming
solutions.description:
## Approach

Build a small dynamic program for choosing exactly three numbers. For each pick count, track both the maximum product and the minimum product seen so far, because multiplying by a negative value can swap best and worst.

## Key Insight

This generalizes the sign-handling idea behind the five-extrema solution. The maximum product after choosing `k` numbers may come from the previous maximum or previous minimum, depending on the sign of the current number.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(1), since there are only four pick counts

tests.description: Exactly three positive numbers multiply directly.
The three largest positives form the maximum.
With exactly three negatives, all must be used.
Two large negatives and the largest positive beat the three largest values.
Zero is better than every negative product.
All-negative arrays maximize by using the three values closest to zero.
Two equal negative extremes with the largest positive form the answer.
Two negatives and the largest positive beat products involving zero.
A single large positive can pair with two most negative values.
A longer all-positive array uses the top three values.
Constraint-bound positive and negative extremes remain within the 32-bit result range.
At the negative boundary, the least negative valid triple is still the maximum.
